extracted.intended_audience: appellate attorneys and practitioners in veterans benefits law (Veterans Court and Federal Circuit litigators), VA adjudicators, and veterans' counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria governing appellate review from the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims to the Federal Circuit, and how VA diagnostic codes are to be identified and applied in rating decisions. Focuses on preservation/forfeiture of arguments, Federal Circuit jurisdictional limits, and interpretation/application of VA rating regulations (e.g., DC 5003, DC 5260, DC 5261).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit jurisdictional limits on Veterans Court review
rubrics_metrics.description: Our authority to review decisions by the Veterans Court is 'limited by statute.' We have jurisdiction where presented with an argument that the Veterans Court's decision 'may have rested on an incorrect rule of law.' Where no constitutional question is presented, the Federal Circuit lacks authority to review the Veterans Court's factual determinations or applications of law to the facts of a particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 38 U.S.C. § 7292 and cases (Perciavalle v. McDonough, Martin v. McDonald). The Court will consider questions of law (including interpretation of statutes or regulations) but will not revisit factual findings or factual applications by the Veterans Court. Jurisdiction exists for contentions about interpretation of a regulation that might alter the Veterans Court's result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veterans Court must make a determination on the legal issue presented
rubrics_metrics.description: The Veterans Court must have made a determination on the legal issue presented to the Federal Circuit—either expressly or implicitly—so that the Federal Circuit can assess whether an incorrect rule of law was applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A determination may be express or implicit (i.e., the Veterans Court's result might be altered by adopting the legal position pressed by appellant). The Federal Circuit can review an interpretation of a regulation urged on appeal when it is a contention about regulatory interpretation that might alter the Veterans Court's result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation / forfeiture rule for appellate arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments not presented to the Veterans Court are forfeited on appeal to the Federal Circuit; failure to present an argument to the Veterans Court is a non-jurisdictional defect that can justify affirmance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least where the veteran had counsel, the Court follows a strong (non-jurisdictional) rule that arguments not presented to the Veterans Court are forfeited. Cases cited: Smith v. Collins, Scarborough v. Principi, Gurley v. McDonough. Forfeiture, not jurisdictional defect, supports affirmance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to present and cite legal authority in Veterans Court to preserve argument
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid forfeiture, a litigant must properly present the contention (and supporting legal authorities) to the Veterans Court; merely mentioning a regulation in footnotes or in a different context does not preserve a new legal theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the appellant's mention of DC 5003 in footnotes as support for different points did not preserve the distinct DC 5003 contention later raised to the Federal Circuit. The Court emphasizes that listing or arguing the regulation as the legal basis in the Veterans Court brief is required to preserve the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and application of 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a, DC 5003 (degenerative arthritis)
rubrics_metrics.description: DC 5003 instructs VA to rate 'degenerative arthritis . . . on the basis of limitation of motion under the appropriate diagnostic codes,' and contains a sentence stating: 'When however, the limitation of motion of the specific joint or joints involved is noncompensable under the appropriate diagnostic codes, a rating of 10 pct is for application for each such major joint or group of minor joints affected by limitation of motion, to be combined, not added under diagnostic code 5003.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appellant argued that DC 5003 requires a 10% rating for limited extension of the knee under certain circumstances even if another DC already yields a 10% rating for the same joint. The interpretation of DC 5003 is a legal question that, if properly presented, could alter the rating outcome; the Court treated it as such for jurisdictional purposes but affirmed based on forfeiture because it was not preserved below.

rubrics_metrics.name: VA duties under 38 C.F.R. § 4.27 and § 4.25(b) when assigning diagnostic codes/ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: VA must exercise care in identifying and selecting the applicable disability code for each condition and must grant separate ratings to separate disabilities that arise from a single disease entity (e.g., arthritis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant invoked these regulatory duties to argue that limitation of flexion and limitation of extension are separate disabilities and should not be conflated; footnotes cited General Counsel precedents were used to support related arguments to the Veterans Court but did not preserve the particular DC 5003 contention raised on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of specific diagnostic codes for knee conditions (DC 5260 / DC 5261) and rating outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: DC 5260 covers limitation of flexion (bending) of the knee and DC 5261 covers limitation of extension (straightening); ratings under these codes are determined by whether the veteran's measured limitation meets the criteria for a compensable evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case the regional office and Board found a 10% rating under DC 5260 for limited flexion and a 0% rating under DC 5261 for limited extension (the Board concluded the extension symptoms did not justify a higher evaluation). The Board also considered whether separate ratings could be assigned under other diagnostic codes and concluded they could not. The decision illustrates that measured range-of-motion findings drive which DC and what percentage rating apply, subject to regulatory rules about combining vs. adding ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to present an argument may be excused by permitting a new claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where an appellant forfeits an argument on appeal, the Court noted the appellant 'may make his DC 5003 argument in a new claim,' indicating that procedural forfeiture on appeal does not bar later administrative re-presentation of the legal theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court cited the appellant's ability to pursue the issue in a new administrative claim as a reason not to overlook forfeiture; this underscores that preservation requirements operate within the appellate pathway but do not necessarily extinguish administrative remedies.
